paras: The lynching of John Tolly was the hanging of a young Black man by a mob at Elizabethtown, Illinois, on the evening of Monday, June 26, 1882. He was accused of trying to break into the house of Mrs. Howe, but she could not identify him, and a witness said he had been elsewhere. Papers across the country carried the story because the man hanged was believed to be innocent, under headlines such as "Hanged the Wrong Man."

According to a man who came down the Ohio River from Elizabethtown and told the Cairo Bulletin he had seen it all, a young Black man came partway through the window of a newly married couple named Howe on Sunday night. Mrs. Howe was alone and screamed, and the intruder struck at her as she ran past and then fled. A Springfield dispatch put the attempt on Saturday night, while the Elizabethtown wire that named the intruder as John Jolly put it on the morning of June 29.

In the Cairo Bulletin's account, Mrs. Howe's father and brothers found "a young boy" walking down the street nearby and brought him back to the house, but she could not say for sure that he was the man. He was jailed all the same, and because her relatives were making threats, the sheriff moved him to the court house so he could be taken by skiff to Golconda for safekeeping. While the sheriff was getting a boat, the father and brothers, named Belt, and "a number of others" took the prisoner out of the court house.

On the way the young man insisted he was innocent and begged for his life, and his aged father pleaded with them too. The informant said the elder Belt knocked him senseless with a gun butt, put a rope around his neck, struck him down again and kicked him in the face, and the party then hanged him from a tree in front of his father. Shorter wire reports said only that he was "brutally beaten" and hanged by a mob, or that a crowd gathered near Mrs. Howe's house and hanged a man taken for Jolly.

The Springfield dispatch said other witnesses, including one who had slept with Tully on Saturday night, testified that he could not have been there, and it predicted that "the guilty party" would soon be caught. The Cairo Bulletin reported that the people of Elizabethtown were "very much excited," but its story breaks off at the bottom of the column, and no report of an inquest, arrests or charges against the lynchers appears in the coverage.

The Cairo Bulletin, the nearest paper, was first, on June 28, calling it "a horrible crime" and "horrible outrage" and turning it against the "good old Republican" state of Illinois. On June 30 the Springfield dispatch ran in the Omaha Bee as "An Innocent Darkey Lynched" and in the New Haven Morning Journal and Courier as "An Innocent Man Mobbed," both saying the mob had "shamefully maltreated" him.

The Jolly version ran in the Washington National Republican as "Hanged the Wrong Man" and later in Wilmington, Somerset, Pennsylvania, and Greenville, Mississippi. The unnamed version appeared in Salt Lake City, Sacramento and Los Angeles, where the Herald placed it at "Elizabeth, N. M." Syndicated weekly news summaries in Iowa and Dakota called the killers "a posse" and noted that Mrs. Howe never identified the man. None of these papers named the lynchers; the Belt name appears only in the Cairo Bulletin.

The papers named the victim differently: the Cairo Bulletin called him John Tolly and the Springfield dispatch John Tully, while the Elizabethtown wire gave the name John Jolly to the intruder and said the man hanged was only "supposed to be Jolly." The Cairo Bulletin's eyewitness has him jailed and taken from the court house, but the wire has a crowd seizing him near the house soon after the break-in. The wire's June 29 date for the break-in conflicts with the Monday evening hanging date given by three separate reports, of which the Cairo Bulletin's is the nearest to the scene and claims an eyewitness.

bases: Every report says a mob or crowd hanged a Black man accused of trying to break into Mrs. Howe's house (A1, A2, A3, A4).

A mob hanged the man without any legal process (A2, A3, A4); A1 says Mrs. Howe's father and brothers 'and a number of others' took him from the court house, and every report says he was killed for an alleged attempted break-in and assault on a woman (A1, A3).
A claimed eyewitness (A1), a Springfield dispatch from mail advices (A2, A8) and two separate Elizabethtown wires (A3, A4) all report the hanging, though they differ on names and timing.

accounts.label: Eyewitness informant (Cairo Bulletin)
accounts.gist: A man came partway through the Howes' window on Sunday night; Mrs. Howe's father and brothers seized a boy in the street whom she could not identify; he was jailed, moved to the court house to be sent to Golconda, and taken out by the Belts and others, who beat him and hanged him in front of his father.

accounts.label: Springfield dispatch (mail advices)
accounts.gist: A mob maltreated and hanged John Tully, a Kentucky negro, Monday night for offering violence to Mrs. John Howe on Saturday night; she could not identify him and an alibi witness said he could not have been there.

accounts.label: Elizabethtown wire (Jolly version)
accounts.gist: John Jolly tried to force his way into Mrs. Howe's house 'this morning' and abused her; soon afterward a crowd seized a negro thought to be Jolly and hanged him, probably the wrong man.

accounts.label: Elizabethtown wire (short version)
accounts.gist: On Monday evening a young colored man thought to have struck a woman who stopped him entering a house was beaten and hanged by a mob; he is believed innocent.

framing.detail: The Cairo Bulletin called it 'a horrible crime' and 'horrible outrage', described the victim's pleas sympathetically, and blamed the 'good old Republican' state of Illinois.
The Omaha Bee ran the Springfield dispatch under 'An Innocent Darkey Lynched', saying the mob 'shamefully maltreated' him while using a racial slur in the headline.
Eastern and western dailies carried the wire under 'Hanged the Wrong Man', 'Lynched the Wrong Man', 'An Innocent Man Lynched', focusing on the mistaken identity rather than the lynching itself.
The syndicated weekly summary said a 'posse' 'brutally beat and then hung' a negro though Mrs. Howe failed to identify him.

conflicts.note: Tolly, Tully and Jolly may be variants of one name; the Jolly wire separates the intruder from the man hanged, while A1 and A2 give the name to the man hanged.
A1, A2 and A4 agree the hanging was Monday evening or night, which rules out the June 29 morning date of the Jolly wire; A1 is the nearest source and claims an eyewitness.
